questions.question: Your loader's memory cache is keyed only by URL. A screen shows the same image as a 48dp avatar and as a full-width header. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing, because Android rescales the cached bitmap automatically at draw time
The header refetches from the network each time, since URL keys never hit
The disk cache and the memory cache end up storing different files for one URL
One decoded size serves both, so the header blurs or the avatar wastes memory
questions.explanation: A decoded bitmap depends on the target size and transformations, not just the source. Including size, transformations and config in the memory cache key keeps variants separate. The disk cache can still be keyed by URL if it stores the original bytes.

questions.question: Roughly how much memory does a 4000 x 3000 photo take when decoded at full size as ARGB_8888?
options: About 12 MB
About 36 MB
About 48 MB
About 4 MB, the same as the JPEG
questions.explanation: ARGB_8888 uses 4 bytes per pixel, so 12 million pixels take about 48 MB no matter how small the compressed JPEG is. This is why a loader must downsample to the view's size (for example with `inSampleSize` or ImageDecoder target sizes) before decoding. 36 MB would be 3 bytes per pixel, which this config does not use.

questions.question: Twenty list cells request the same image at the same size at once. You dedupe them onto one in-flight decode. What must happen when one cell is recycled and cancels?
options: Cancel the shared job at once, so no decoding work is wasted on recycled cells
Detach that cell only; cancel the job when every waiter has cancelled
Ignore cancellation for shared jobs and let every registered callback fire anyway
Restart the shared job, so the remaining cells receive a fresh decode result
questions.explanation: A shared job needs reference counting: each subscriber can leave, but the work continues while anyone is still waiting. Cancelling on the first leave starves the other 19 cells, and ignoring cancellation would deliver images into recycled views. Restarting wastes the progress already made.

questions.question: In a fast-scrolling RecyclerView, cells briefly show the wrong image before the right one appears. What is the usual root cause in the loader?
options: The memory cache is too small, so images are evicted and come back in random order
Decoding runs on a background thread instead of on the main thread
The recycled view's old request isn't cancelled, so its late result lands
The LRU is built on a LinkedHashMap that iterates in access order
questions.explanation: A loader must bind each target to its current request and cancel or ignore the previous one when the view is rebound. Otherwise a slow earlier response overwrites the view after it has been reused. Background decoding is correct, and access-ordered LinkedHashMap is the standard LRU building block.

questions.question: A bitmap memory cache should be bounded by the number of entries, for example "keep the last 100 bitmaps".
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Bitmaps vary hugely in size, so 100 thumbnails and 100 full-screen images use very different memory. Bound the cache by bytes, measuring each entry with `allocationByteCount`, and size the budget from the app's available memory.

questions.question: Why did some modern Android image loaders, such as Coil 2, drop bitmap pooling?
options: `inBitmap` was removed from BitmapFactory, so reusing pixel memory is impossible
Bitmaps taken from a pool cannot be drawn by Compose's Image composable at all
Pooling only ever helped on 32-bit devices, which modern loaders no longer support
Pixels live in native memory since Android 8, so gains are small and reuse bugs costly
questions.explanation: Pooling mattered when pixel data was on the Java heap and every decode caused GC churn. With pixels in native memory and hardware bitmaps that cannot be reused anyway, the gain is small, while returning a bitmap to the pool that is still on screen causes corrupted images. `inBitmap` still exists; it is just less worth using.

questions.question: Which are sound choices for an image loader's disk cache? Select all that apply.
options: Store image bytes in SharedPreferences as Base64 for simplicity
Bound the cache by total bytes and evict least recently used entries
Store the original downloaded bytes so other sizes can be decoded without refetching
Read from disk on the main thread, since flash storage is fast enough
Write to a temporary file and atomically rename it into place once complete
questions.explanation: Atomic rename means a crash mid-write never leaves a half-written file that later decodes as corrupt. A byte-bounded LRU keeps disk use predictable, and caching originals lets you serve any target size. SharedPreferences loads its whole file into memory, and disk reads on the main thread can still stall frames.

questions.question: A Fragment loads images into its views. Which lifecycle should the loader tie those requests to?
options: The Fragment's `viewLifecycleOwner`, since views die while it sits on the back stack
The Fragment's own lifecycle, since it is created first and outlives all of its views
The Activity's lifecycle, so requests survive Fragment transactions and replacements
The process lifecycle, so images can keep loading in the background between screens
questions.explanation: A Fragment on the back stack keeps its lifecycle but destroys its view, so requests tied to the Fragment itself keep holding and updating dead views. The view lifecycle cancels them at `onDestroyView`. Activity or process scope makes the leak worse.

questions.question: A bitmap decoded with `Bitmap.Config.HARDWARE` can be read pixel by pixel with `getPixel()` on the CPU, just slower.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: False. Hardware bitmaps keep their pixels only in GPU memory, so CPU pixel access throws an exception. A loader must decode to a software config when a transformation (blur, palette extraction) needs pixel access.

questions.question: Users report a list sometimes shows the wrong variant of an image (for example the uncropped version where a circle crop was requested). Which loader bugs can cause this? Select all that apply.
options: A recycled view's previous request is not cancelled when it is rebound
Decoding runs on Dispatchers.IO instead of Dispatchers.Default
The memory cache key ignores the transformations applied
The LRU evicts entries in least-recently-used order
questions.explanation: If transformations are not part of the key, a cropped and an uncropped image collide in the cache. A stale request landing on a reused view also puts the wrong image on screen. LRU eviction order and the choice of background dispatcher affect performance, not correctness of which image appears.
